awd_abstract_narration:
The project addresses directly the heart of algebraic topology: computing invariants like numbers, groups, and rings to understand spaces. The goal of algebraic topology is to systematically build a connection between algebraic objects like numbers and geometric objects like spaces. This connection allows a two-way flow of information, with algebraic invariants distinguishing spaces and topological methods informing algebraic problems. Starting from foundational work of Quillen, algebraic and algebraic geometry data like formal groups gives rise to new invariants for spaces with striking properties. This project combines this classical thread with much more recent developments coming from equivariant algebraic topology. "Equivariant algebraic topology" remembers a collection of symmetries inherent in a space as part of the data, systematically grouping spaces with the same symmetries, and the numbers and invariants produced must reflect this. This extra structure provides more nuanced computations, giving more information about how the classically described invariants change under symmetries. Equivariant algebraic topology has experienced a renaissance recently due to the solution by the PI, Hopkins, and Ravenel to the Kervaire Invariant One problem, one of the oldest outstanding problems in algebraic topology. The solution introduced a host of new constructions and techniques that have striking ramifications in classical and equivariant algebraic topology, and this project focuses on unpacking some of these new constructions, exploring their ramifications in classically studied computations, and describing what they mean for algebraic topology in general. Many of the projects focus on diversity in STEM. Building on the PI's prior First Year seminar on Women in Math, the PI will create a diversity-driven class, combining mathematical content and pedagogy with discussions of representation and inclusion in mathematics. At the same time, the PI intends to create more opportunities for students who do not see themselves as "math people" to connect with algebra and geometry concepts using UCLA's "Maker Spaces" to have students design and build concrete models. The PI will continue conference organizing, especially conferences focusing on making space for early career mathematicians and for advanced undergraduates, using these as a way to connect students with the ideas and researchers in stable homotopy.



Using newly developed tools in equivariant stable homotopy, the PI will study the slice spectral sequences for certain chromatically meaningful quotients of hyperreal spectra. These are closely connected to the classical approaches to studying K(n)-local phenomena using the Hopkins--Miller higher real K-theory spectra, and at the prime 2, computations here subsume all previously known higher real K-theory computations. The project focuses mainly on concrete computations (both of chromatically meaningful quotients of hyperreal bordism and of more traditional objects like the dual Steenrod algebra), while also studying more abstract questions of what kinds of multiplicative structures we can see. Finally, an application of all of this machinery to the classical questions of orientability of vector bundles is explored.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Algebraic topology studies the ways one can attach invariants like numbers or more general algebraic objects to spaces in a way that reveals intrinsic features. In the mid 20th century, algebraic topologist shifted focus to better understanding how these invariants themselves interact, starting with the development of "stable homotopy theory". This paradigm shift allowed tools from disciplines like algebraic geometry to be imported and reinterpreted in algebraic topology, with homotopical notions of commutative rings playing a central role. 

The notion of homotopy usually destroys symmetries present in a space, and choosing to keep track of some particular groups of symmetries is the domain of equivariant homotopy theory. This area has been a core subfield in algebraic topology, with most of the big results in algebraic topology using equivariant techniques. Computations here tend to be significantly harder than non-equivariant computations, and this is in part due to much richer algebraic structure arising for the natural invariants. 

In the solution to the Kervaire Invariant One Problem, Hopkins, Ravenel, and the PI introduced two new tools to equivariant homotopy theory: the multiplicative norm and the slice filtration. Many projects in this grant directly engage with these tools, pushing our understanding both of equivariant homotopy theory and of how to work with the objects.

In work with Beaudry, Lawson, Shi, and Zeng, the PI produced equivariant lifts of Morava K-theories, showing how these are particularly amenable to slice spectral sequence computations. In studying this, unexpected classically motivated questions involving the dual Steenrod algebra, viewed as a highly structured ring spectrum, arose, since the slice computations could be recast in this non-equivariant language. This culminated in work of the PI and Lawson studying more general questions of multiplicatively killing classes in a highly structured ring, the solution for which unified many previous observations in the area. Equivariant versions of commutative ring spectra, developed by Blumberg and the PI, are parameterized by combinatorial data: a transfer system. In work with Li and Meng, the PI counted the number of compatible transfer systems for an arbitrary cyclic p-group. In work with Blumberg and Lawson, the PI recast the slice filtration into a more general version that underscores multiplicative features connected to equivariant commutativity.

While originally developed to study equivariant homotopy groups, the slice filtration can instead study any equivariant homology theory. In work with Carrick and Ravenel, the PI developed this notion, showing how this approach could be used to study the ordinary homology of the fixed points of the truncated Real Brown-Peterson spectra. These computations suggested that these fixed points were always fp spectra in the sense of Mahowald-Rezk, and Carrick and the PI showed this more generally. Similarly, using slice filtration arguments together with multiplicative considerations, Hopkins and the PI showed how to compute with a general version of the equivariant dual Steenrod algebra.

The grant supported the work of five graduate students. They worked on projects generalizing equivariant homotopy theory to a kind of category-equivariance; building new versions of Dunn additivity for equivariant operads; studying equivariant Thom spectra and structured maps between them; understanding the operadic structure on certain spectral algebraic geometry problems; and working the the cotangant complex in equivariant algebra.

The PI has been an active conference organizer. Over the course of the grant, the PI co-organized 7 conferences, special sessions, and summer schools in the US and abroad. The PI gave a series of lectures at various conferences, from an introduction to equivariant homotopy theory at CIMAT-Merida to a lecture series on equivariant operads. Finally, the PI gave a general audience talk at the Isaac Newton Institute.
